technique.name: Raycasting
technique.description: A ray projected from the user intersects a target for fast distal selection.
technique.best: Fast selection of visible distant targets.
technique.limits: Small and occluded targets can be difficult; precision decreases with distance.
technique.how: Point a virtual ray at an object and confirm with a button, pinch, or dwell.
technique.citation: Mine, M. (1995). Virtual environment interaction techniques. UNC Chapel Hill CS Dept, 2.

technique.name: Virtual Hand
technique.description: A direct 3D selection technique where the user controls a virtual hand to touch, grab, and manipulate nearby objects in the virtual environment.
technique.best: Natural selection and manipulation of nearby objects, especially when the interaction benefits from proprioception and direct hand-object contact.
technique.limits: Less suitable for distant targets because the user must reach toward the object or rely on an extended mapping. It can also cause fatigue during repeated or long interactions.
technique.how: Move the tracked hand or controller so that the virtual hand overlaps with the target object, then confirm the selection by grabbing, pressing a button, or performing a pinch gesture.
technique.citation: Mine, M. R., Brooks Jr, F. P., & Sequin, C. H. (1997, August). Moving objects in space: exploiting proprioception in virtual-environment interaction. In Proceedings of the 24th annual conference on Computer graphics and interactive techniques (pp. 19-26).

technique.name: Cone Casting
technique.description: A cone-shaped volume expands the effective acquisition area for remote targets.
technique.best: Distant targets when exact ray alignment is demanding.
technique.limits: May create ambiguity when several candidates fall inside the cone.
technique.how: Aim a cone at a region; resolve the chosen object by proximity or ranking.
technique.citation: Liang, J., & Green, M. (1994). JDCAD: A highly interactive 3D modeling system. Computers & graphics, 18(4), 499-506.

technique.name: Bubble Cursor
technique.description: An adaptive cursor expands until it encloses the nearest available target.
technique.best: Dense scenes with many small selectable objects.
technique.limits: Can feel unpredictable when target positions change quickly.
technique.how: Move the cursor near a target; the selection region adapts to isolate it.
technique.citation: Vanacken, L., Grossman, T., & Coninx, K. (2007, March). Exploring the effects of environment density and target visibility on object selection in 3D virtual environments. In 2007 IEEE symposium on 3D user interfaces. IEEE.

technique.name: Gaze + Pinch
technique.description: Gaze identifies an intended object and a pinch confirms the action.
technique.best: Hands-busy contexts and lightweight XR input.
technique.limits: May suffer from Midas-touch effects without deliberate confirmation.
technique.how: Look at a candidate target, then pinch to select it.
technique.citation: Pfeuffer, K., Mayer, B., Mardanbegi, D., & Gellersen, H. (2017, October). Gaze+ pinch interaction in virtual reality. In Proceedings of the 5th symposium on spatial user interaction (pp. 99-108).

technique.name: VoiceRay
technique.description: Ray-based selection enhanced with ordinal voice commands to resolve ambiguity.
technique.best: Dense and clustered distant objects where raycasting is ambiguous.
technique.limits: Speech latency and social or contextual appropriateness can matter.
technique.how: Aim at a cluster, then say an ordinal command such as “third”.
technique.citation: Turkmen, R., Rasoulifar, Z., & Batmaz, A. U. (2026, April). VoiceRay: 3D Object Selection Technique for Occluded and Dense Environments in Virtual Reality. In Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (pp. 1-19).

technique.name: Aperture Selection
technique.description: Targets are acquired through a controllable aperture that balances precision and speed.
technique.best: Precise selection of small or distant objects.
technique.limits: Requires learning and can add extra adjustment steps.
technique.how: Adjust an aperture around the intended target, then confirm.
technique.citation: Forsberg, A., Herndon, K., & Zeleznik, R. (1996, November). Aperture based selection for immersive virtual environments. In Proceedings of the 9th annual ACM symposium on User interface software and technology (pp. 95-96)..

technique.name: Volumetric Hand Cursor
technique.description: A 3D cursor volume attached to the hand enables direct spatial selection.
technique.best: Near-field selection and embodied manipulation.
technique.limits: Arm fatigue and occlusion can increase in long sessions.
technique.how: Move a hand-aligned cursor volume to intersect a target, then pinch.
technique.citation: Lopes, D. S., de Figueiredo Parreira, P. D., Paulo, S. F., Nunes, V., Rego, P. A., Neves, M. C., ... & Jorge, J. A. (2017). On the utility of 3D hand cursors to explore medical volume datasets with a touchless interface. Journal of biomedical informatics, 72, 140-149.

technique.name: Gaze + Voice
technique.description: Gaze narrows the candidate set while voice specifies the final intended item.
technique.best: Highly ambiguous scenes, especially when targets overlap.
technique.limits: Depends on reliable speech recognition and concise labels.
technique.how: Look toward the target group and speak a target name or ordinal.
technique.citation: Bashar, M. R., Mutasim, A. K., Pfeuffer, K., & Batmaz, A. U. (2026, April). Eyes on Many: Evaluating Gaze, Hand, and Voice for Multi-Object Selection in Extended Reality. In Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (pp. 1-14).

technique.name: Go-Go
technique.description: A direct 3D selection and manipulation technique that extends the user's virtual reach using a non-linear mapping between the real hand and the virtual hand.
technique.best: Selecting and manipulating objects that are beyond normal arm reach while preserving the feeling of direct hand-based interaction.
technique.limits: The non-linear hand mapping can reduce precision and may require practice, especially when switching between near objects and extended-reach objects.
technique.how: Move the tracked hand toward the target. For nearby objects, the virtual hand follows the real hand closely. After a threshold distance, the virtual hand moves farther than the real hand, allowing the user to reach distant objects without physically walking.
technique.citation: Poupyrev, I., Billinghurst, M., Weghorst, S., & Ichikawa, T. (1996). The Go-Go Interaction Technique: Non-Linear Mapping for Direct Manipulation in VR. Proceedings of the 9th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology, 79–80.

technique.name: Flexible Pointer
technique.description: A flexible 3D pointing technique that bends the pointer path, allowing users to select fully or partially obscured objects in augmented and virtual reality environments.
technique.best: Selecting objects that are partially hidden, visually occluded, or difficult to reach with a straight ray-based pointing technique.
technique.limits: The curved pointer may require additional control and can be harder to understand than simple raycasting, especially when users need to adjust the pointer shape precisely.
technique.how: The user controls a virtual pointer whose shape can bend around occluding objects. Instead of pointing only along a straight line, the pointer can curve toward a target that is not directly visible or not easily reachable with standard egocentric pointing.
technique.citation: Olwal, A., & Feiner, S. (2003). The Flexible Pointer: An Interaction Technique for Selection in Augmented and Virtual Reality. UIST '03 Conference Supplement, ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology, 81–82.

technique.name: HOMER
technique.description: A remote object selection and manipulation technique that combines ray-based selection with hand-centered manipulation after the object is grabbed.
technique.best: Grabbing and manipulating remote objects in immersive virtual environments without requiring the user to physically travel to the object.
technique.limits: The transition from ray-based selection to hand-centered manipulation can require practice, and remote manipulation may reduce precision compared with direct nearby manipulation.
technique.how: Point a ray at a remote object and confirm the grab. Once selected, the object is attached to the user's virtual hand so it can be moved and manipulated through hand or controller motion.
technique.citation: Bowman, D. A., & Hodges, L. F. (1997, April). An evaluation of techniques for grabbing and manipulating remote objects in immersive virtual environments. In Proceedings of the 1997 Symposium on Interactive 3D Graphics (pp. 35-ff).

technique.name: Depth Ray
technique.description: A 3D selection technique for volumetric displays that extends ray-based pointing by adding control over depth, allowing users to select targets located inside a true 3D volume.
technique.best: Selecting objects in volumetric displays where targets may appear at different depths and where a simple 2D cursor or direct 3D point cursor can be inefficient.
technique.limits: It is designed specifically for volumetric display interaction, so its usefulness may depend on the display hardware and the available input device. Users also need to control both pointing direction and target depth.
technique.how: The user points toward the target region and adjusts the selection depth along the ray until the intended volumetric target is reached, then confirms the selection.
technique.citation: Grossman, T., & Balakrishnan, R. (2006, October). The design and evaluation of selection techniques for 3D volumetric displays. In Proceedings of the 19th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (pp. 3–12).

technique.name: PORT
technique.description: A 3D multiple object selection technique that allows users to select a group of objects in an immersive virtual environment using a spatial region-based interaction.
technique.best: Selecting multiple objects at once, especially when targets are grouped, clustered, or when selecting objects one by one would be inefficient.
technique.limits: The technique can become less precise when objects are densely packed or when intended and unintended objects are close to each other within the selection region.
technique.how: The user specifies a spatial selection region around the desired objects. Objects that fall within the defined region are selected as a group, reducing the need for repeated single-object selections.
technique.citation: Lucas, J. F. (2005). Design and evaluation of 3D multiple object selection techniques. Doctoral dissertation, Virginia Tech.

technique.name: SQUAD
technique.description: A progressive refinement technique for rapid and accurate 3D selection, where the system repeatedly narrows a group of candidate targets until the intended object can be selected.
technique.best: Selecting small, dense, or distant targets when many objects are close together and a single pointing action may not be accurate enough.
technique.limits: SQUAD may require multiple refinement steps, so it can be less efficient for simple targets that can be selected directly. It is most useful when the initial selection is ambiguous.
technique.how: The user first indicates a group of possible targets. The system divides the candidate set into smaller groups, and the user repeatedly chooses the group containing the intended target until the final object is selected.
technique.citation: Kopper, R., Bacim, F., & Bowman, D. A. (2011). Rapid and accurate 3D selection by progressive refinement. In 2011 IEEE Symposium on 3D User Interfaces (3DUI). IEEE.

technique.name: Expand
technique.description: A 3D selection technique for dense and dynamic virtual environments that temporarily expands the candidate objects so the user can select one target more easily.
technique.best: Selecting small, dense, or moving objects in game-based virtual environments where targets are close together and difficult to acquire with standard pointing.
technique.limits: The technique changes the visual arrangement of candidate objects during selection, which may interrupt the original spatial layout. It is most useful when selection accuracy is more important than preserving the scene exactly during the selection step.
technique.how: The user first indicates a dense group of possible targets. The system then expands or spreads the candidate objects apart, making them easier to distinguish and select. After the user selects the intended target, the environment can return to its normal arrangement.
technique.citation: Cashion, J., Wingrave, C., & LaViola Jr, J. J. (2012). Dense and dynamic 3D selection for game-based virtual environments. IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics, 18(4), 634–642.

technique.name: Silk Cursor
technique.description: A 3D target acquisition technique that uses a semi-transparent cursor to reduce visual occlusion and help users acquire targets in 3D space.
technique.best: Selecting or acquiring 3D targets when cursor visibility and target visibility both matter, especially in dynamic 3D scenes where an opaque cursor could hide the target.
technique.limits: Transparency can make the cursor less visually salient, and the technique depends on careful visual design so users can still judge the cursor's position and relation to the target.
technique.how: The user controls a semi-transparent 3D cursor and moves it toward the target. Because the cursor is partially transparent, the user can see target geometry through or behind the cursor while aligning the cursor for acquisition.
technique.citation: Zhai, S., Buxton, W., & Milgram, P. (1994). The “Silk Cursor”: Investigating transparency for 3D target acquisition. In Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '94), 459–464.

technique.name: GazeBubble
technique.description: A 3D gaze-pointing technique that adapts the bubble cursor mechanism to gaze-based target acquisition in virtual reality.
technique.best: Hands-free selection of 3D targets in virtual reality, especially when gaze can quickly indicate the intended region or candidate target.
technique.limits: Gaze-based pointing can be affected by eye-tracking precision, visual attention demands, and ambiguity when many targets are close together.
technique.how: The user points with gaze, and the system applies a bubble-like selection mechanism around the gaze position to determine the most likely target. In dense scenes, an assistive interaction such as Diffuse can help separate or clarify candidate targets.
technique.citation: Zhang, B., Sun, M., Li, Z., Jin, Y., & Tian, Y. (2026). GazeBubble: Exploring bubble mechanism for 3D gaze pointing to enhance target acquisition in virtual reality. International Journal of Human–Computer Interaction, 42(4), 2132–2163.

technique.name: Wise Cursor
technique.description: An assisted 3D selection technique for mouse-driven serious games that estimates which object the user intended to select and supports clarification when the intended target is uncertain.
technique.best: Improving accessibility and usability in 3D serious games, especially for users who are not experienced with first-person 3D interaction.
technique.limits: The technique depends on the quality of the candidate-ranking model. When the system's probability estimate does not match the user's intention, an additional clarification step may be needed.
technique.how: When the user clicks in the 3D environment, the system computes a set of candidate objects and estimates the probability that each one is the intended target. If one candidate is sufficiently likely, it is selected; otherwise, the system asks the user to clarify the selection.
technique.citation: Moya, S., Grau, S., & Tost, D. (2013). The Wise Cursor: Assisted selection in 3D serious games. The Visual Computer, 29(6), 795–804.

technique.name: MultiFingerBubble
technique.description: A 3D bubble cursor variation for dense environments that uses multiple fingers to support target acquisition in crowded 3D spaces.
technique.best: Selecting targets in dense 3D environments where several objects are close together and a single-point cursor may not provide enough control or precision.
technique.limits: The technique depends on reliable hand and finger tracking. It may also require users to coordinate multiple fingers, which can increase motor complexity compared with single-point selection.
technique.how: The user performs selection with multiple tracked fingers. The system uses a bubble-cursor-like mechanism around the fingers to identify and acquire the intended target among nearby candidates.
technique.citation: Delamare, W., Daniel, M., & Hasan, K. (2022, April). MultiFingerBubble: A 3D bubble cursor variation for dense environments. In CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems Extended Abstracts (pp. 1–6).

technique.name: Bubble Raycasting
technique.description: A ray-casting variation that integrates a bubble mechanism to improve 3D target acquisition in virtual reality.
technique.best: Selecting small, dense, or difficult-to-point-at targets in VR when standard ray-casting requires too much precision.
technique.limits: The bubble mechanism can introduce ambiguity when several targets are close to the ray or fall within the adaptive selection region.
technique.how: The user points toward the target with a ray. Instead of selecting only the exact ray intersection, the system applies a bubble-like selection region around the ray to determine the most likely target.
technique.citation: Lu, Y., Yu, C., & Shi, Y. (2020, March). Investigating bubble mechanism for ray-casting to improve 3D target acquisition in virtual reality. In 2020 IEEE Conference on Virtual Reality and 3D User Interfaces (VR) (pp. 35–43). IEEE.

technique.name: Bubble Gaze Cursor
technique.description: A gaze-based area cursor technique that applies the bubble cursor mechanism to eye-gaze interaction, enlarging the effective selection area around the gaze point.
technique.best: Selecting small or closely spaced targets with eye gaze when direct gaze pointing is difficult due to eye-tracking noise or limited gaze precision.
technique.limits: The technique can still become ambiguous when multiple targets are close to the gaze point, and gaze jitter may affect which object is treated as the nearest candidate.
technique.how: The user looks toward the desired target. The system places a bubble-like area cursor around the gaze position and selects the nearest or most likely target inside the adaptive selection area.
technique.citation: Choi, M., Sakamoto, D., & Ono, T. (2020, June). Bubble Gaze Cursor + Bubble Gaze Lens: Applying area cursor technique to eye-gaze interface. In ACM Symposium on Eye Tracking Research and Applications (pp. 1–10).

technique.name: Bubble Gaze Lens
technique.description: A gaze-based selection technique that combines the bubble cursor idea with a lens mechanism to support more accurate target selection through eye gaze.
technique.best: Selecting small or dense targets with gaze when users need additional visual support to distinguish the intended target from nearby alternatives.
technique.limits: The lens can add visual complexity and may be less suitable when the interface should remain visually minimal or when targets move quickly.
technique.how: The user looks toward a target region. The system activates a lens around the gaze position, helping reveal, enlarge, or clarify nearby candidate targets so the intended one can be selected more accurately.
technique.citation: Choi, M., Sakamoto, D., & Ono, T. (2020, June). Bubble Gaze Cursor + Bubble Gaze Lens: Applying area cursor technique to eye-gaze interface. In ACM Symposium on Eye Tracking Research and Applications (pp. 1–10).
